strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: pre-trained VLM representations lack sensitivity to robotic control signals, and the proposed RS-CL provides a simple, lightweight, self-supervised solution that requires no additional curated datasets or training stages.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple settings: fine-tuning on top of a strong SOTA VLA (GR00T N1.5) on RoboCasa-Kitchen and LIBERO, from-scratch training on diverse VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, SigLIP2, GR00T VLM), and real-robot experiments on a 7-DoF Franka arm with in-domain and generalization tasks.

Consistent and often substantial performance gains across nearly all settings, particularly on pick-and-place tasks requiring precise positioning (30.8%->41.5% on RoboCasa PnP), and real-robot close-lid task under occlusion, supporting the core claim that proprioceptive alignment improves precision-critical manipulation.

Solid ablation studies isolating the contribution of the soft-label weighting scheme (vs. plain InfoNCE, vs. alternative distance targets) and the view-cutoff augmentation (vs. other cutoff variants), which help substantiate design choices rather than just reporting an ensemble improvement.

Quantitative representation analysis using CKNNA provides direct evidence that RS-CL increases alignment between learned embeddings and proprioceptive states, strengthening the causal story connecting the method to the observed downstream gains.

Comparison against alternative VLM-adaptation strategies (RoboBrain, VeBrain, Cosmos-Reason1, NORA) shows RS-CL is more effective and complementary to these robotics-pretrained backbones, adding to the significance of the contribution.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details (algorithm box, hyperparameters, dataset sources, training/eval protocols) and an honest limitations section acknowledging exclusion of other modalities (object pose, contact force).
weaknesses: Real-robot experiments use small sample sizes (24 trials per task, 60 demonstrations per task) and no variance/confidence intervals or multiple seeds are reported for either simulation or real-world results, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains, especially the smaller ones (e.g., LIBERO improvements of ~0.7-1%).

The method introduces several hyperparameters (λ schedule, τ, β, projector dimension, summarization token) but sensitivity to these choices is only partially explored (mainly ablations on soft-label target and augmentation type); no ablation on λ schedule shape, τ, or β is provided despite these plausibly having significant impact on the weighted contrastive loss.

The core novelty is somewhat incremental: combining supervised contrastive learning (weighted InfoNCE, following Khosla et al. and Suresh & Ong) with proprioceptive-state-based soft labels and a straightforward view-masking augmentation; the individual components are adaptations of well-established techniques rather than fundamentally new ideas, which affects originality strength.

Comparisons to prior representation-learning approaches specifically tailored for robot manipulation (e.g., R3M, VIP, TCN referenced in Related Work) are absent from the main experiments, leaving open whether RS-CL's specific proprioceptive-state weighting is meaningfully better than these established alternative contrastive schemes when applied in the same VLA pipeline.

The choice of Euclidean distance over proprioceptive states (position, rotation, gripper) as the similarity metric is somewhat ad hoc; different state components have different scales/units, and no discussion or ablation addresses normalization or relative weighting across these heterogeneous dimensions.

Some benchmarks show only marginal gains (e.g., LIBERO improves from 95.7% to 96.4% average, and some individual RoboCasa tasks like 'Object' suite in LIBERO regress from 99.4 to 98.6), suggesting the method's benefits may be concentrated in precision-demanding pick-and-place scenarios rather than being universally beneficial, which is not fully reconciled in the discussion.

The real-robot generalization results (Fig. 5b) show relatively modest absolute improvements (e.g., visual: 25.0->31.2%, physical: 20.8->29.2%) with unclear statistical reliability given the small trial counts, tempering claims of strong generalization benefits.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing, supported by a compelling qualitative visualization (Fig. 2) showing that pre-trained VLM embeddings are dominated by visual appearance rather than task-relevant/control signals, and that RS-CL fixes this.

The proposed RS-CL is simple, lightweight (operates purely at the representation level via a summarization token and adapter/projector, no extra VLM forward passes), and integrates into standard flow-matching VLA training as an auxiliary loss with minimal overhead.

Broad and fairly thorough empirical validation: results span two simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa-Kitchen, LIBERO) across multiple demonstration budgets, real-robot experiments with in-domain and generalization (visual/physical/language) tasks, and from-scratch training across seven different VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, further-trained variants, SigLIP2 frozen/unfrozen, GR00T N1.5 VLM).

Consistent, non-trivial improvements are reported in essentially every setting tested, including notable gains on pick-and-place tasks requiring precise positioning (30.8%→41.5% on RoboCasa PnP), and on real-robot tasks (45.0%→58.3%).

Useful ablations disentangle the contribution of the contrastive framework itself (plain InfoNCE) versus the proprioceptive-state soft-weighting scheme, and compare several augmentation strategies and soft-label distance targets, supporting the design choices with evidence rather than assertion.

A quantitative representation-alignment analysis (CKNNA) is included to directly substantiate the claim that RS-CL better aligns representations with proprioceptive states, beyond just downstream task success.

The paper positions RS-CL against a relevant and current set of alternative strategies (further training VLMs on embodied-reasoning/grounding data: RoboBrain, VeBrain, Cosmos-Reason1, NORA), showing RS-CL is complementary to and often exceeds these more data/compute-intensive approaches.
weaknesses: No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for any of the main quantitative tables (Tables 1, 2, 5-10) or the real-robot trials, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (some of which are only 1-3 points) are statistically robust versus run-to-run noise, especially given single-run simulation policies can have high variance.

The main fine-tuning headline results (Table 1, 2, and real-robot experiments) are built almost entirely on a single VLA architecture (GR00T N1.5); although π0/π0-FAST are shown as separate baselines for context, RS-CL is never actually combined with these alternative action-decoder architectures, leaving open whether the benefit generalizes across different generative action-decoder designs beyond DiT-based GR00T.

In the from-scratch experiments, absolute success rates are very low across the board (roughly 2%-21%), which weakens the practical significance of the reported relative improvements and makes it harder to be confident the ranking of methods would hold at higher performance regimes typical of deployed systems.

The method's core idea (supervised/weighted InfoNCE using auxiliary distances as soft labels) is a fairly direct combination of existing techniques (Khosla et al. 2020; Suresh & Ong 2021) applied to a new signal (proprioceptive-state distance); the technical novelty is therefore incremental relative to the empirical contribution.

The Euclidean-distance-based state similarity (Eq. 4) mixes heterogeneous quantities (Cartesian position, 6D rotation, gripper state) without discussion of normalization or scale balancing, which could make the soft-weighting scheme sensitive to unit choice and is not analyzed or justified.

Real-robot in-domain evaluation uses a modest 24 trials per task, and generalization results are reported without any measure of variance, limiting confidence in the magnitude of reported real-world gains.

The paper does not empirically compare against other established contrastive representation-learning baselines for robot control that are cited in related work (e.g., R3M, VIP, time-contrastive networks), which would have better contextualized RS-CL's benefit relative to prior contrastive approaches rather than only against VLA-specific fine-tuning strategies.

strengths: Simple, lightweight, and easy-to-integrate method: RS-CL operates purely at the representation level (adding a summarization token, a projector, and an auxiliary contrastive loss), requiring no additional training stages or curated robotics-specific datasets, and is compatible with standard VLA training pipelines.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: results span multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa-Kitchen with 30/100/300 demos, LIBERO across 4 suites), real-robot experiments (in-domain pick-and-place, close-lid task, and generalization to visual/physical/language shifts), and from-scratch training on many different VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, SigLIP2 frozen/unfrozen, GR00T N1.5 VLM), showing consistent gains.

Meaningful and consistent improvements, particularly on tasks requiring precise positioning (pick-and-place success improves substantially, e.g., 30.8%->41.5% on RoboCasa and 45.0%->58.3% on real robot), supporting the paper's central claim about proprioceptive grounding aiding precise control.

Good ablations and interpretability: soft-label target ablation (current state vs. next action distance) and augmentation ablation (view cutoff vs. alternative cutoffs) are informative and support design choices; CKNNA analysis directly measures representation alignment to proprioceptive states, providing a mechanistic explanation beyond just downstream task success.

Comparison against alternative VLM-adaptation strategies (embodied-reasoning fine-tuned VLMs, discretized action pretraining) is a valuable contextualization showing RS-CL's gains are complementary and often larger, strengthening the significance of the contribution.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, dataset sources, and extensive appendix details for both simulation and real-world protocols are provided.
weaknesses: Real-robot evaluations use small trial counts (24 trials per task) and modest demonstration counts (60 demos), which limits statistical confidence in the reported real-world gains, especially given the relatively large error bars implied by such small samples; no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed reporting is given anywhere in the paper for either simulation or real-world results, making it hard to assess the significance of moderate gains (e.g., LIBERO improvements are small, ~0.7 points).

The method's benefit appears to interact strongly with backbone trainability and batch size (e.g., LIBERO CL results are flat due to smaller batch size, SigLIP2 frozen backbone barely improves), suggesting the approach's practical effectiveness may be sensitive to training/batch configuration in ways not fully characterized or discussed as a core limitation.

The choice of using only proprioceptive end-effector/joint state as the contrastive supervision signal (versus richer signals like object pose or contact) is acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically explored even in a preliminary way, leaving open how much the specific choice of state signal matters versus just having *some* smooth state-based auxiliary signal.

The paper's core hypothesis (VLM embeddings dominated by visual appearance rather than robot state) is illustrated only qualitatively via a single task visualization (Fig. 2); a more rigorous quantitative pre-training baseline analysis of representation gaps would strengthen the motivation section.

Some comparisons (e.g., against embodied-reasoning fine-tuned VLM baselines in Fig. 7) combine differences in backbone scale, training data, and adaptation objective, making it harder to cleanly attribute the performance gap solely to the RS-CL mechanism versus confounds in baseline training recipes.

strengths: Extensive and rigorous empirical validation: the method is tested on two simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa-Kitchen, LIBERO), real-robot experiments with in-domain and multiple generalization axes (visual, physical, lighting, language), across many VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, SigLIP2, GR00T N1.5, further-trained robotics VLMs like RoboBrain, VeBrain, Cosmos-Reason1, NORA), and across different action-decoding paradigms (flow-matching GR00T/π0 and autoregressive π0-FAST), showing consistent gains in nearly all settings.

Strong and consistent quantitative improvements, including new SOTA on RoboCasa-Kitchen (69.7%), pronounced gains on precision-critical pick-and-place tasks (+11.2%), and real-robot success rate improvements (45.0%→58.3%).

Thorough ablations and analysis: soft-label target choice, augmentation strategy comparisons (view cutoff vs. token/span/feature cutoff), hyperparameter sensitivity study (Table 8) showing robustness, and a well-designed comparison against Time-Contrastive Networks showing better efficiency and performance.

Insightful qualitative and quantitative representation analyses (t-SNE visualizations, KNN task-phase classification, CKNNA alignment metric) that support the central claim that pretrained VLM embeddings are dominated by visual appearance rather than control-relevant signal, and that RS-CL meaningfully improves this alignment.

The method is lightweight and practical: minimal computational overhead (+1.25% wall-clock time) is explicitly quantified, and the design (representation-level augmentation, single added token) is compatible with existing single-stage VLA training pipelines without requiring extra VLM forward passes or curated datasets.

Broad robustness checks in the appendix, including different proprioceptive state parameterizations (EEF pose vs. joint position), higher-dimensional embodiments (bimanual dexterous hands, humanoid), and task-wise breakdowns explaining where gains concentrate.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a fairly straightforward combination of existing ideas (supervised contrastive learning with soft weighting by state distance, akin to Suresh & Ong 2021; a cutout-style representation augmentation borrowed from Shen et al. 2020) applied to a new domain; the novelty is more in application and engineering than in fundamental algorithmic innovation.

Real-robot evaluation uses relatively small trial counts per task (24 trials) with no reported variance/statistical significance, and success rates for both baseline and RS-CL remain modest in absolute terms (e.g., ~29-58%), making it hard to assess how reliable the observed gains are versus noise.

Gains on some benchmarks/tasks are marginal (e.g., LIBERO overall 95.7%→96.4%, open-and-close tasks on RoboCasa show near-zero or even slightly negative change), suggesting the benefit is task-dependent and the paper could more directly discuss when/why the method might not help.

The paper freezes the VLM backbone by default (following GR00T N1.5 practice) while much of the related work it cites emphasizes that training the backbone jointly with action prediction is important for VLA performance; the interaction between RS-CL and backbone fine-tuning is only lightly explored (one SigLIP2 unfrozen ablation), leaving open how RS-CL compares/combines with the dominant full-finetuning paradigm at scale.

Baseline comparisons in Table 1 mix reproduced and originally-reported numbers from different sources/papers, which could introduce inconsistencies in evaluation protocol (e.g., differing seeds, trial counts, or hyperparameters) that are not fully controlled for.
